paragraphs: Even Alyosha himself was taken by surprise at being called. He was not required to take the oath, and I remember that both sides questioned him very gently and kindly. Clearly his reputation for goodness had gone before him. Alyosha gave his evidence modestly and with restraint, but his warm sympathy for his unhappy brother could not be mistaken. Asked to describe his brother’s character, he said Mitya was perhaps hot-tempered and swept away by his passions, but also honorable, proud and generous, and capable of sacrificing himself if need be. He admitted, though, that his brother’s passion for Grushenka and his rivalry with their father had put him in an unbearable position lately. But he rejected with indignation the suggestion that his brother might have committed murder for money. He did recognize that the three thousand roubles had become almost an obsession with Mitya. Mitya saw it as part of the inheritance his father had cheated him of, and although he was normally indifferent to money, he could not even speak of that three thousand without fury. As for the rivalry between the two “ladies,” as the prosecutor put it, meaning Grushenka and Katya, he answered evasively, and on one or two questions he refused to answer at all.
“Did your brother tell you, at any rate, that he meant to kill your father?” asked the prosecutor. “You may decline to answer if you think it necessary,” he added.
“He didn’t tell me so directly,” answered Alyosha.
“What do you mean? Did he tell you indirectly?”
“He once spoke to me of his hatred for our father, and of his fear that at an extreme moment ... in a moment of fury, he might murder him.”
“And you believed him?”

“I’m afraid I did. But I never doubted that some higher feeling would save him at the fatal moment, and it did save him, because he did not kill my father,” Alyosha said firmly, in a loud voice that carried through the whole court.
The prosecutor started like a war-horse hearing a trumpet.

“Let me assure you that I fully believe your conviction is completely sincere. I do not put it down to your affection for your unhappy brother, nor confuse the two. Your peculiar view of this whole tragic affair is already known to us from the preliminary investigation. I won’t try to hide from you that it is highly individual and contradicts all the other evidence the prosecution has collected. So I think it essential to press you: what facts have led you to this conviction of your brother’s innocence, and of the guilt of another person, the one you named in your evidence at the preliminary inquiry?”
“I only answered the questions I was asked at the preliminary inquiry,” replied Alyosha, slowly and calmly. “I made no accusation against Smerdyakov on my own.”
“But you did give evidence against him?”

“I was led to it by my brother Dmitri’s words. I was told what happened at his arrest, and how he pointed to Smerdyakov, before I was questioned. I believe absolutely that my brother is innocent, and if he didn’t commit the murder, then—”
“Then Smerdyakov did? Why Smerdyakov? And why are you so completely convinced of your brother’s innocence?”
“I can’t help believing my brother. I know he wouldn’t lie to me. I could see from his face that he wasn’t lying.”
“Only from his face? Is that all the proof you have?”
“I have no other proof.”
“And you have no proof at all of Smerdyakov’s guilt, except your brother’s word and the look on his face?”
“No, I have no other proof.”

The prosecutor dropped his questions at that point. Alyosha’s evidence left the public bitterly disappointed. There had been talk about Smerdyakov before the trial. Someone had heard one thing, someone else had noticed another. People said that Alyosha had gathered some extraordinary proofs of his brother’s innocence and Smerdyakov’s guilt. And after all that there was nothing, no evidence at all except certain moral convictions, which are only natural in a brother.

But now Fetyukovitch began his cross-examination. He asked Alyosha when the prisoner had spoken to him of hating his father and possibly killing him, and whether Alyosha had heard it, say, at their last meeting before the catastrophe. Alyosha gave a start as he answered, as though he had just then remembered and understood something.
“I remember something now that I’d completely forgotten myself. It wasn’t clear to me at the time, but now—”

And, clearly struck by an idea for the first time only now, he eagerly told how at his last meeting with Mitya that evening, under the tree on the road to the monastery, Mitya had struck himself on the chest, “the upper part of the chest.” He had said several times that he had a way of recovering his honor, and that this way was here, here on his chest. “When he struck himself on the chest, I thought he meant it was in his heart,” Alyosha went on. “I thought he meant he might find strength in his heart to save himself from some awful disgrace that was waiting for him, and that he didn’t dare confess even to me. I must admit that at the time I did think he was talking about our father, and that the disgrace he was shuddering at was the thought of going to our father and doing him some violence. Yet just then he was pointing at something on his chest. I remember the thought struck me that the heart isn’t in that part of the chest but lower down, and that he was striking himself much too high, just below the neck, and kept pointing at that spot. My idea seemed silly to me then, but perhaps he was pointing to that little bag with the fifteen hundred roubles in it!”
“Just so,” Mitya cried from his place. “That’s right, Alyosha, it was the little bag I hit with my fist.”

Fetyukovitch hurried over to Mitya and begged him to keep quiet, and in the same moment he turned and pounced on Alyosha. Alyosha was carried along by his own memory, and he eagerly offered his theory that the disgrace was probably just that fifteen hundred roubles he carried. Mitya could have returned it to Katerina Ivanovna as half of what he owed her. But he had made up his mind not to repay her and to spend it on something else, namely on running away with Grushenka, if she would consent.

“That’s it, it must be!” exclaimed Alyosha, in sudden excitement. “My brother cried out several times that he could free himself at once from half of the disgrace, half of it (he said _half_ several times), but that he was so unhappy in his weakness of will that he wouldn’t do it ... that he knew beforehand he was incapable of doing it!”
“And you remember clearly and confidently that he struck himself on exactly this part of the chest?” Fetyukovitch asked eagerly.

“Clearly and confidently. I thought at the time, ‘Why is he striking himself up there when the heart is lower down?’ and the thought seemed stupid to me then ... I remember that it seemed stupid ... it flashed through my mind. That’s what brought it back to me just now. How could I have forgotten it until now? It was that little bag he meant when he said he had the means but wouldn’t give back the fifteen hundred. And when he was arrested at Mokroe he cried out—I know, I was told it—that he considered it the most disgraceful act of his life that he had the means of repaying Katerina Ivanovna half (half, note!) of what he owed her, and still couldn’t bring himself to repay it, and preferred to stay a thief in her eyes rather than part with the money. And what torture, what torture that debt has been to him!” Alyosha exclaimed in conclusion.

The prosecutor, of course, objected. He had Alyosha describe once more how it had all happened, and several times he pressed the question: “Had the prisoner seemed to point to anything? Or had he perhaps simply thumped himself on the chest with his fist?”
“But it wasn’t with his fist,” cried Alyosha. “He pointed with his fingers, and he pointed here, very high up.... How could I have forgotten it so completely until this moment?”

The President asked Mitya what he had to say about the last witness’s evidence. Mitya confirmed it. He said he had been pointing to the fifteen hundred roubles on his chest, just below the neck, and that this was of course the disgrace. “A disgrace I can’t deny, the most shameful act of my whole life,” cried Mitya. “I could have repaid it and I didn’t. I preferred to stay a thief in her eyes rather than give it back. And the most shameful part of it was that I knew beforehand I wouldn’t give it back! You’re right, Alyosha! Thank you, Alyosha!”

So Alyosha’s cross-examination came to an end. What mattered about it, and what struck everyone, was that at least one fact had come to light. It was only one tiny scrap, a mere hint of evidence, but it went some small way toward proving that the bag had really existed and had held fifteen hundred roubles. It suggested that the prisoner had not been lying at the preliminary inquiry when he claimed at Mokroe that the fifteen hundred roubles were “his own.” Alyosha was glad. With a flushed face he went back to the seat set aside for him. He kept repeating to himself: “How was it I forgot? How could I have forgotten it? And what made it come back to me now?”

Katerina Ivanovna was called to the witness-box. As she came in, something extraordinary went through the court. The ladies seized their lorgnettes and opera-glasses. The men stirred, and some got to their feet for a better look. Afterwards everybody swore that Mitya had turned “white as a sheet” at the sight of her. She was dressed all in black, and she walked forward modestly, almost timidly. Her face gave no sign that she was agitated, but a resolute light shone in her dark and gloomy eyes. I may add that many people remarked how especially handsome she looked at that moment. She spoke softly but clearly, so that the whole court heard her. She kept her composure, or at least tried to seem composed. The President began his questions with tact and great respect, as though afraid of touching “certain chords,” and he was considerate of her great unhappiness. But in reply to one of the first questions, Katerina Ivanovna said firmly that she had once been engaged to the prisoner, “until he left me of his own accord...” she added quietly. When they asked her about the three thousand she had trusted Mitya to post to her relations, she said firmly, “I didn’t give him the money simply to send it off. I felt at the time that he was in great need of money.... I gave him the three thousand on the understanding that he should post it within the month if he cared to. There was no need for him to worry about that debt afterwards.”
I will not repeat every question put to her and every answer in detail. I will give only the substance of what she said.

“I was firmly convinced that he would send off that sum as soon as he got money from his father,” she went on. “I have never doubted his disinterestedness and his honesty ... his scrupulous honesty ... in money matters. He felt quite certain that he would receive the money from his father, and he spoke to me about it several times. I knew he had a feud with his father, and I have always believed that his father treated him unfairly. I don’t remember any threat he made against his father. He certainly never made any such threat in front of me. If he had come to me at that time, I would have set his mind at rest at once about that unlucky three thousand roubles. But he had stopped coming to see me ... and I myself was put in such a position ... that I couldn’t invite him.... And in fact I had no right to be demanding about that money,” she added suddenly, and there was a ring of resolution in her voice. “I once owed him more than three thousand for help he gave me in money, and I took it, although at that time I couldn’t foresee that I would ever be in a position to repay my debt.”
